newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian bonds open weaker on employment data.
newsitem.headline: Canadian bonds open weaker on employment data.

text.p: Canadian bonds opened mostly weaker on Friday as nervous investors dumped positions on news of a sharp drop in Canada's unemployment rate and renewed fears of a looming interest rate hike, analysts said.
Statistics Canada reported that the unemployment rate dropped to 9.1 percent in June from 9.5 percent in May.
A Reuters survey of economists had predicted a drop to 9.3 percent in June.
Canada's employment growth increased by 51,500 in June, slightly below May's figure of 61,000 but above market expectations of an increase of 38,800.
"The numbers are definitely weighing on the shorter end of the curve, and that's why we're having some curve flattening," said Harvinder Kalirai, Canadian analyst with New York-based I.D.E.A.
"It (the data) has increased expectations of a Bank of Canada rate hike later in the year," Kalirai added.
Canada's 10-year benchmark bond fell C$0.12 to C$109.14 to yield 6.008 percent, compared to its U.S. equivalent which dipped 2/32 to yield 6.26 percent.
The negative spread between the bonds remained at 25 basis points, the same as at the close of trading on Thursday.
Analysts said a stronger Canadian dollar, which rallied on Canada's employment numbers, failed to offset growing bearish sentiment in the bond market.
Canada's dollar opened at C$1.3689 (US$0.7305) in heavy trade on Friday from C$1.3733 (US$0.7282) at Thursday's close.
"The real issue for the bond market today is the obvious strength of the Canadian economy," said Doug Porter, senior economist at Toronto brokerage Nesbitt Burns.
"This morning's employment numbers speak for themselves. Obviously, the economy is in the midst of a very powerful growth phase," Porter added.
A Reuters U.S. survey forecast that producer prices would be unchanged in June from a drop of 0.3 percent in May.

But bond markets received some good news on Friday with the release of a Nesbitt Burns report suggesting Canada had stopped new borrowing for the first time in 25 years, with the federal government issuing no new bonds a year earlier than expected.
Porter said a possible shortage of new bonds in Canada should translate into a long-term bullish trend for the Canadian bond market.
"It should make the kinds of gains we've seen in bonds the last couple of years a permanent feature," Porter said.
Canada's benchmark 30-year long bond rose C$0.25 to C$118.54 to yield 6.574 percent.
The U.S. 30-year bond gained 6/32 to yield 6.55 percent.
The spread between the two benchmark bonds moved to a spread of two basis points, the same as at the close on Thursday.
The three-month cash T-bill yielded 3.17 percent against its U.S. equivalent, which yielded 5.13 percent.
((Paul Simao, Reuters Toronto Bureau (416) 941-8104))
